newsitem.title: VIETNAM: Peterson crowns career of war and peace in Vietnam.
newsitem.headline: Peterson crowns career of war and peace in Vietnam.

text.p: Douglas "Pete" Peterson's arrival in Hanoi on Friday to become the first United States ambassador to a post-war Vietnam brings the career of a one-time Vietnam War fighter pilot and prisoner of war full circle.

Considered a genial and fair-minded man, the 61-year-old former congressman has made it clear that he returns with no grudges about a conflict that cost some 58,000 American lives and 6-1/2 years of his own youth in a Vietnam prison.
Asked recently whether he would like to meet any of the jailers from the euphemistically named "Hanoi Hilton" prison, Peterson replied: "It would be an interesting conversation."
Peterson says he has not decided whether the war was a mistake, but vows to build a bridge across a "river of pain" left after the Communist victory over U.S.-backed forces in 1975.
Nebraska-born Peterson -- a widower and father of a son and a daughter -- began his involvement with Vietnam 31 years ago as a Thailand-based U.S. Air Force pilot.

On September 10, 1966, on his 67th mission, Peterson's aircraft was shot down over North Vietnam's Red River delta. He bailed out and had an inglorious landing in a mango tree beside an irrigation ditch halfway between Hanoi and Haiphong port.
Two villagers who found Peterson stripped him of all but his underclothes and marched him to a local storehouse, where he was guarded until officials came to take him away.

"I didn't get much of an impression of him," says one of his captors, Nguyen Viet Chop, who is now 69. "When we made him walk, I saw he was much taller than me and fatter. His toes were very fat too."
Peterson was locked up in the "Hanoi Hilton" -- which, in a sign of the times, has been transformed into a swanky hotel and office complex -- until his repatriation in 1973.
After retirement from the air force in 1980, he headed a construction firm and, in 1983, founded a computer company, CRT Computers.

He also worked as an administrator of a rehabilitation programme for troubled adolescents, before being elected to Congress for the first time in November, 1990. There, as a Democrat, he represented Florida's second district, which includes the state capital, Tallahassee.
Re-elected in 1992 and 1994, he was a member of the House of Representatives for six years.
During that time, Peterson served as co-chairman of the U.S.-Russia Joint Commission on POW/MIAs, working to obtain information about U.S. servicemen still listed as missing in action (MIA).
Furthering efforts to account for the 2,124 American personnel still listed as missing in Indochina from the war, 1,585 of them in Vietnam, will be his priority task as ambassador in Hanoi.

He will also be charged with speeding up progress towards a bilateral trade accord, which has moved at a glacial pace since Vietnam and the United States normalised relations in July 1995, and chipping away at old suspicions.
